clinicalPearls: Multiple small (a few millimetres), discrete, sharply defined porcelain-white macules, most numerous on the sun-exposed extensor forearms and shins
Prevalence and lesion number increase with age and cumulative sun exposure, making it very common in the elderly
Lesions are asymptomatic, remain stable and do not coalesce, unlike vitiligo
Essentially a clinical diagnosis; dermoscopy shows well-defined hypopigmented patches and biopsy is rarely needed
Reduced but not absent melanocytes and melanin distinguish it from the complete pigment loss of vitiligo
On Wood lamp the macules are off-white rather than the chalky, sharply fluorescent white of vitiligo
Largely a cosmetic concern; photoprotection may limit progression and most cases need no treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis reflects a localised reduction in the number and activity of epidermal melanocytes with decreased melanin production, so pigment is diminished rather than absent. Cumulative ultraviolet exposure and skin ageing are the principal contributors, with a possible genetic predisposition. The result is scattered focal areas of reduced epidermal melanisation on chronically photodamaged skin.
additionalInvestigations: Wood-lamp examination to compare with the chalky white of vitiligo
Potassium hydroxide microscopy to exclude pityriasis versicolor
Assessment of cumulative sun exposure and photodamage
Skin biopsy only when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain
redFlags: Rapidly spreading or coalescing depigmentation that should prompt reconsideration of vitiligo
Associated cutaneous sclerosis or atrophy suggesting lichen sclerosus or morphoea
New scaling or symptomatic lesions suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign, stable and permanent, with individual macules persisting indefinitely; it carries no health risk and is purely a cosmetic issue.
pitfalls: Confusing the stable small macules with early vitiligo
Subjecting patients to unnecessary or aggressive treatment
Missing pityriasis versicolor as an alternative cause of hypopigmentation
Attributing spreading depigmentation to idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis
management: Reassure that the condition is benign, stable and carries no health risk, so treatment is optional and purely cosmetic
Advise sun protection with broad-spectrum sunscreen and photoprotective measures to limit the cumulative ultraviolet damage that drives new lesions
Confirm the clinical diagnosis and distinguish it from vitiligo and pityriasis versicolor using Wood-lamp examination and dermoscopy, reserving biopsy for genuine uncertainty
Offer cosmetic camouflage for the porcelain-white macules where appearance is a concern

Consider topical calcineurin inhibitors or retinoids, or localised procedures such as superficial cryotherapy, dermabrasion, fractional laser or targeted phototherapy, counselling on limited and variable benefit
Refer to dermatology only for diagnostic uncertainty or persistent cosmetic concern
